changes.before: Create an `li` from the input text and append it to `#books`.
changes.after: Add and remove one list item while leaving unrelated page content alone.

before: The Document Object Model, or DOM, is the browser's object representation of the page. Each element is a node that JavaScript can read or change. A list element can be the parent of several list-item nodes. Creating an element does not display it yet; you must attach it to an element already on the page.

`document.createElement("li")` creates a new list-item element. The string li is an HTML tag name, not the item's text. Assign `.textContent` to set its title as plain text, then call `.append(item)` on the chosen list to attach it. Append adds a node at the end; if the node already belonged elsewhere, append moves it instead of making a copy.

``` `ul` creates an unordered list, and li creates an entry. The ids distinguish the lists. A selector like `"#books li"` means li elements inside the books element. That space describes an element inside another element; it is part of the selector string.

`querySelector` returns the first matching element or null. `querySelectorAll` returns a collection of matching nodes. `Array.from(...)` makes an array from that collection so you can use array methods. `.find(...)` calls a callback on entries and returns the first for which it returns true, or undefined if none matches. `li => li.textContent === title` asks whether an item's text matches the requested title.

Your project needs addBook and removeBook with the supplied titles. Add Small Worlds to the books list and remove Cloud Atlas from that same list. The other list's Keep me entry must survive. Count one item for each li node, and use selectors scoped to books so unrelated items are not touched. The function's job is a page update; it need not return a title to perform that update.
after:
The DOM is the browser's object model of a page. An element is a node in that model, and it can contain child nodes.

Creating an element does not show it yet. Attach it to the page to make it visible.

`createElement("li")` makes a list item. Set its `textContent`, then append it to the chosen list.

`append` puts a node at the end. If that node was already elsewhere, it moves the node instead of copying it.

Use two lists so you can see which one changes: ```html
  • River Tales
  • Leave this here
``` `ul` is a list, and `li` is a list item. `"#books li"` selects list items inside the element whose ID is books.

`querySelectorAll` gets the matching nodes. `Array.from` puts them in an array.

`find` returns the first item whose callback gives true, or undefined if none matches. Here, the callback compares each item's text with the requested title.

Complete `addBook` and `removeBook`. Keep the call adding Small Worlds, then call `removeBook("Cloud Atlas")`.

Use selectors inside `#books` so the other list's Keep me entry survives. These functions change the page; they do not need to return a title.

In `removeBook`, search only `#books li` for the first matching title.
Check that Keep me in the other list stays untouched.
